purpose: The last untested classification-argument KEEPs. platform-* and compliance-* were deferred as CONVERT ('external objectives, blind evict-A/B is the wrong instrument') and never A/B'd, unlike react/python/quality/ui/cross-cutting. Neither family bundles a runnable check — their 'Checks' sections are prose pointing at external tools (gitleaks, actionlint, axe, semgrep). This run isolates whether that prose changes answer quality beyond the base model. SCOPE: 5 platform-* + 5 soft compliance-* (security, privacy, accessibility, auditability, vulnerability-management). compliance-gdpr and compliance-hipaa are deliberately EXCLUDED and held as the strong external-legal-objective keeps (specific article/safeguard citations, high cost-of-miss). Routing/effect-boundary cases stay in high_use_cases.json; this file is quality cases only and is deliberately not parsed by validate_registry.py.

arms.A_control: Reads the skill's registry/<skill>/SKILL.md guidance and applies it to the scenario.
arms.B_bare: Capable bare model, same scenario, no skill, forbidden from reading registry/ or docs/.
arms.C_substitute: Arm B plus docs/platform-compliance-substitute-note.md, which names ONLY the deterministic external tools/checks each family points at (no prose method). Runs only as a recovery test on cases where mean(A) - mean(B) > 0.15 — i.e. tests whether naming the tool recovers the gap without the prose (the CONVERT hypothesis).

protocol: Blind answer + blind deterministic-anchor scoring (evals/family_ab.workflow.js). Each case 3x per arm in fresh context; answering and scoring are separate agents; the scorer sees only prompt + answer + anchors, never the arm label. Score 0-1: (fraction of must_include satisfied) minus 0.34 per must_exclude present, floored at 0. Exclude degenerate reps and note them.

gate.evict_if: mean(B) >= mean(A) - 0.10 AND no B-only must_exclude violation where A has none
gate.convert_if: a case where mean(A) - mean(B) > 0.25 AND arm C recovers it (meanC >= meanA - 0.10) flags that skill as CONVERT (keep the tool pointer as a thin objective, drop the prose), not a blanket keep. A B-only must_exclude violation on a safety anchor (secret leak, injection, dropped rollback) is itself a CONVERT signal: keep the guardrail.
gate.note: compliance-gdpr / compliance-hipaa are out of scope this run and kept regardless of result.

cases.prompt: Our deploy job runs the test suite and then, in the same job, rebuilds the Docker image and pushes it straight to production. A reviewer says to split it up. Why does this matter, and how should the pipeline be shaped instead?
must_include: promote the exact tested artifact: build once, test that artifact, then deploy the same immutable artifact rather than rebuilding for prod
separate/least-privilege permissions or credentials between the test/PR stage and the deploy stage (deploy gated on the checks that validated the artifact)
must_exclude: endorses rebuilding the image at deploy time so what ships was never the thing that was tested
ignores workflow permission or credential scoping entirely

cases.prompt: A contributor opened a PR from their fork. Our integration tests need a real API key to run. How do we set CI up so those tests can run without creating a security hole?
must_include: recognizes that exposing repository secrets to untrusted fork PR code is the core risk and isolates untrusted PR validation from any secret-bearing job (e.g. gated/approved runs, a separate trusted workflow, or no secret on the fork path)
uses scoped/short-lived credentials or withholds the real secret from fork-triggered runs (e.g. run full integration only after maintainer approval or on trusted branches)
must_exclude: hands the real secret directly to fork PR code with no isolation or approval gate
recommends pull_request_target-style patterns that run untrusted checked-out code with secrets available, without noting the danger

cases.prompt: One deploy ships a DB migration that adds a NOT NULL column plus the app code that writes it. Our rollback plan is just 'redeploy the previous image.' Is that a safe rollback plan?
must_include: identifies that coupling a backward-incompatible schema change with the code in one deploy breaks the rollback: redeploying the old image leaves old code against the new schema (or a half-applied migration)

recommends expand/contract (backward-compatible steps: add nullable, backfill, then enforce) and decoupling/ordering schema vs code deploys so each step is independently reversible or forward-compatible
must_exclude: treats 'redeploy the previous image' as a sufficient rollback despite the incompatible/irreversible schema change
ships schema and code together with no expand-contract, forward-compatibility, or migration reversibility consideration

cases.prompt: We need to roll out a risky change to our high-traffic checkout service. What deployment strategy should we use, and how do we decide during the rollout whether it's safe to continue or to pull it back?
must_include: proposes a progressive strategy (canary / blue-green / percentage ramp) rather than switching everyone at once, with a smoke/health check after deploy
defines objective go/no-go signals (error rate, latency, SLO) and an explicit rollback or roll-forward trigger tied to those signals
must_exclude: recommends a big-bang all-at-once cutover for a change described as risky and high-traffic
gives no measurable promotion criteria or rollback trigger — 'watch it and see'

cases.prompt: Staging runs SQLite and an in-memory job queue; production runs Postgres and SQS. We keep shipping bugs that only appear in production. What's the underlying issue and what should we change?
must_include: names environment / dev-prod parity as the root cause: the backing services differ, so staging cannot catch the class of bugs that depend on the real service semantics
recommends matching the backing-service types across environments (or the closest feasible equivalents) so staging exercises the same behavior as prod
must_exclude: ignores the backing-service divergence as the cause
only suggests 'test more' or 'add logging in prod' without addressing parity

cases.prompt: We want an ephemeral preview environment spun up automatically for each pull request. What do we need to think about for its configuration, data, and lifecycle?
must_include: environment-specific runtime configuration and isolation: no production secrets or production data in previews; config injected per environment
lifecycle management: previews are ephemeral with automatic teardown/expiry, seeded with synthetic or anonymized non-prod data
must_exclude: reuses production data or production credentials inside preview environments
leaves previews with no teardown/expiry (unbounded cost and exposure sprawl)

cases.prompt: During an outage a teammate fixed the load balancer by editing it directly in the AWS console. All our infra is managed in Terraform. What's the concern now, and what should we do?
must_include: identifies configuration drift: real infrastructure state now diverges from the Terraform code, and the next apply will fight or revert the manual change
recommends reconciling the change back into code (import/update the module to match, then plan/apply) and discouraging out-of-band console changes going forward (plan+review / GitOps)
must_exclude: endorses leaving the manual console change permanently outside of code
tells them to just run terraform apply without first reconciling the drift into the code (which would clobber the fix or corrupt state)

cases.prompt: We're setting up Terraform for three environments (dev, staging, prod) with a small team. How should we structure state and modules?
must_include: isolates state per environment (separate state files/backends) so a prod change cannot blast-radius dev/staging, with remote state and locking
reusable modules parameterized per environment, with a plan/review-before-apply flow and least-privilege credentials for prod
must_exclude: puts all three environments in one monolithic shared state
applies to prod with no plan/review step or with broad long-lived static credentials

cases.prompt: To make onboarding faster I put our real staging database password and API keys into .env.example so new devs can just copy the file. Is that a good idea?
must_include: no: .env.example is checked into the repo, so this commits real secrets — real credentials must never live in committed files; keep only placeholder/shape in .env.example and inject real values from a secret manager / runtime
the already-exposed credentials must be treated as leaked: rotate/revoke them now (and scan history), since committing is disclosure
must_exclude: approves putting real secret values in .env.example or any committed file
omits that the exposed credentials must be rotated/revoked after being committed

cases.prompt: Where should our production API keys live, and how should the service actually get them at runtime? We deploy on Kubernetes.
must_include: stored in a secret manager or Kubernetes Secret (ideally external-secrets/CSI rather than baked into the image) and injected at runtime, not build time
least-privilege scoping, redaction in logs, and a preference for short-lived/rotatable credentials or workload identity/OIDC over static long-lived keys
must_exclude: bakes the secrets into the container image or build artifact
commits production secrets to the repo or logs them in plaintext

cases.prompt: This endpoint runs: db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ' + req.params.id). Is this fine? What should I check for across the rest of the app?
must_include: identifies SQL injection and requires parameterized queries / prepared statements (bound parameters), not string concatenation of request input
generalizes to reviewing untrusted-input trust boundaries across the app (other injection sinks: queries, shell, templates, etc.)
must_exclude: claims manual escaping or input validation alone is a sufficient substitute for parameterized queries
treats it as a cosmetic/style nit rather than an exploitable vulnerability

cases.prompt: We're adding a password-reset-by-email flow. What security properties does it need to have?
must_include: single-use, expiring, high-entropy tokens delivered out-of-band, and invalidating sessions / the token after use
resistance to account enumeration (uniform responses regardless of whether the email exists) and rate limiting/throttling on the request and verify steps
must_exclude: reveals whether an account exists (user enumeration) or returns the reset token/new password in the response body
uses long-lived or reusable reset tokens, or embeds the secret token where it gets logged

cases.prompt: Our analytics team wants to log the full HTTP request body for every request to help with debugging. The body includes email, home address, and payment fields. Any privacy concerns?
must_include: invokes data minimization / purpose limitation: don't log sensitive personal or payment data wholesale just for convenience; log only what the purpose needs
requires redaction/tokenization of sensitive fields plus retention limits and access restriction on whatever is logged
must_exclude: approves logging full PII / payment data for debugging convenience
ignores minimization, retention, and access-control concerns entirely

cases.prompt: We're building 'export my data' and 'delete my account' features for account settings. What should each actually cover to be done correctly?
must_include: export returns the personal data actually held about the user in a portable/readable form, sourced across the systems that hold it

deletion genuinely removes or anonymizes the data across stores — including backups, logs, derived datasets, and data shared with third parties — with verification and explicit handling of legal-retention exceptions
must_exclude: implements deletion as only a soft-delete/flag while retaining the personal data indefinitely with no anonymization
ignores copies in backups, logs, analytics, or third-party processors

cases.prompt: We built a custom dropdown menu out of clickable <div>s with onClick handlers. It looks great but QA says it isn't accessible. What's wrong and how should we fix it?
must_include: the control is not keyboard operable and lacks semantics: use a native element (<button>/<select>) or correct ARIA roles/states (e.g. role, aria-expanded) with real focus management
full keyboard support (tab to reach, arrow/enter/escape to operate), an accessible name, and a visible focus indicator
must_exclude: fixes only the visuals or adds a click handler without making it keyboard operable or semantically labeled
suggests hiding it from assistive tech (aria-hidden / removing from the a11y tree) as the fix

cases.prompt: What accessibility checks should we run on a new signup form before we ship it, and which of those can we automate versus do by hand?
must_include: covers programmatic labels/associations, error identification and messaging, focus order + visible focus, and color contrast, anchored to WCAG success criteria
distinguishes what automated tooling can catch (axe/lint/contrast checker) from what needs manual or assistive-technology testing (screen-reader pass, keyboard walkthrough)
must_exclude: claims an automated scan alone is sufficient proof of accessibility
omits keyboard/focus or contrast from the checklist

cases.prompt: For a SOC 2 audit we've been asked to show who approved and who deployed each production change. Right now we just merge PRs to main. What evidence should we be producing?
must_include: durable change records that link each change to its approver, deployer, timestamp, and the deployed artifact (PR approval + CI evidence + deploy log + artifact identity)
traceability from the originating requirement/ticket through the merged change to the production deploy, with the records protected from tampering
must_exclude: asserts that raw git history alone is sufficient with no approval, deploy, or actor evidence
proposes evidence that is editable/untraceable (no immutability, no actor attribution)

cases.prompt: We're adding an admin action that lets a support agent refund any customer. What should we record about it for auditability?
must_include: an append-only audit record of who did what to whom and when: actor identity, target customer, amount, reason/authorization basis, and time
the record is tamper-resistant and retained so the action can be reconstructed and reviewed later
must_exclude: records only that 'a refund happened' with no actor, target, or authorization detail
uses a mutable log the acting admin could later alter, or writes sensitive data (full card number) into the trail

cases.prompt: Dependabot just opened 40 alerts on our repo. Do we have to fix all of them right now? How should we decide what to do with them?
must_include: prioritize by exploitability/reachability and exposure (is the vulnerable code path actually used and reachable, is it internet-facing) combined with severity — not by raw alert count or CVSS alone
a triage process with proportionate SLAs: remediate, defer with an explicit risk-acceptance decision, or accept — and record the decision as evidence
must_exclude: says fix everything immediately by count with no prioritization, or dismisses all alerts as noise
ranks purely on CVSS severity ignoring whether the vulnerable path is reachable/used

cases.prompt: A critical CVE just dropped for a library we depend on. Walk me through how we should respond.
must_include: first assess whether and how we're actually affected — the installed version and whether the vulnerable path is reachable/exposed — before acting
remediate (patch/upgrade/mitigate) on a timeline matched to the assessed risk, then verify the fix closed it (re-scan / test) and record the closure evidence
must_exclude: patches blindly or panics without checking whether the code is actually affected
closes the alert with no verification or re-scan that the vulnerability is actually resolved
